Medicaid / mental-health care / 4–6 min

What does it take to get
mental-health care
through Medicaid?

A provider directory makes care look findable. What happens when someone tries to use it?

By Megan Quigley · A synthesis of published research

Follow the story ↓

From a coverage card to an appointment

01 Coverage02 Directory03 Calls04 Waits05 Access

01 / Coverage

Covered

Medicaid covers mental-health services. Coverage is the beginning of access.

This story follows adult psychiatric prescribing care: from a directory listing to an appointment offer.

Medicaid.gov: managed-care delivery ↗Medicaid.gov: behavioral-health services ↗

02 / Directory

Listed

Researchers sampled 80 listed clinicians in each of four cities: New York City, Los Angeles, Chicago, and Phoenix.

All were listed as accepting new patients in the city’s highest-enrollment Medicaid managed-care plan.

320 listings. The test was whether a call could secure an appointment.

JAMA: audit methods and results ↗

03 / Calls

Contacted

Start with the same 320 offices. Watch the listings separate into the outcomes of the calls.

57 offered the selected clinician. Another 30 offered an alternate. At 233 offices, no appointment was obtained.

87 offers out of 320 calls: 27.2%. An offer is not a completed visit.

JAMA: four-city Medicaid appointment audit ↗

04 / Waits

Waiting

An appointment offer brings another question: when?

In NYC, 36.3% of sampled offices offered an appointment with any clinician. The median recorded wait was 28 days.

This is one plan’s sample of adult psychiatric prescribing offices—not all NYC care. Waits were missing for 17 offers across the four cities.

JAMA: wait times and missing observations (Figure 1) ↗

05 / Access

Accountable

A useful directory should lead to reachable, available, timely care.

A separate federal review recommended improving Medicaid directory accuracy. That recommendation is not a measured improvement.

When the first office cannot help, who helps the patient find the next one?

HHS inspector general: Medicaid directory-accuracy recommendation ↗

What this story can tell us

This is an audit of adult psychiatric prescribing appointments in four cities, with calls in 2023. It is not a national rate, a study of every form of therapy, or a record of completed treatment. The study did not include a commercial-insurance comparison group.

Illustrations explain a process. They do not depict an interviewed person. Recommendations and editorial questions are labeled separately from measured results.
